5. DISCUSSÃO
O carcinoma hepatocelular (CHC) e o hepatoblastoma (HB) são tumores
primários do fígado com etiologias distintas. Enquanto o CHC está associado a processos
crônicos de dano e inflamação na fase adulta, o HB está relacionado a alterações no
desenvolvimento hepático durante a infância (Pio et al., 2025; Villanueva, 2019) . Em
ambos os casos, a complexidade TME e a eficácia limitada de terapias direcionadas
exclusivamente às células tumorais destacam a importância de estratégias que também
considerem o compartimento estromal. Nesse contexto, a doxazosina surge como uma
candidata ao reposicionamento por apresentar efeitos tanto antitumorais quanto anti -
fibróticos, atuando também sobre células do estroma. Sendo assim, esta tese teve como
objetivo investigar o papel do TME, com ênfase nas HSCs, na modulação da resposta
terapêutica, bem como avaliar o potencial da doxazosina em modelos 3D de câncer
hepático. Nossos resultados indicam que esse fármaco pode interferir em mecanismos de
escape metabólico e estrutural nos tumores estudados.
A necessidade de investigar abordagens terapêuticas mais abrangentes, como as
propostas nesta tese, reflete o impacto crescente das neoplasias hepáticas em termos
epidemiológicos e econômicos. Em escala global, os dados do Global Cancer
Observatory (GLOBOCAN) posicionam o câncer de fígado como a sexta neoplasia mais
incidente e a terceira principal causa de morte relacionada ao câncer no mundo,
responsável por mais de 800 mil óbitos anuais (Bray et al., 2024; Mauro et al., 2025). No
Brasil, além da recém-publicada Estimativa 2026-2028 do Instituto Nacional de Câncer
(INCA) prever o alarmante registro de 781 mil novos casos de câncer por ano no país ,
com o câncer de fígado sendo destacado entre as neoplasias de maior incidência em
regiões de alta vulnerabilidade, o impacto financeiro da doença é devastador (Martins et
al., 2026). Estudos recentes de farmacoeconomia estimam que o câncer de fígado impõe

92

ao Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) um custo total que ultrapassa os R$ 600 milhões anuais,
englobando tanto os gastos diretos de alta complexidade (internações e transplantes
hepáticos) quanto os indiretos associados à mortalidade prematura (Zambeli, 2025) .
Embora seja considerado uma doença rara na população geral, o HB representa o tumor
hepático primário mais comum na infância. Nesse contexto, o prognóstico de pacientes
pediátricos que desenvolvem tumores resistentes à cisplatina permanece como um desafio
clínico crítico. D iante da eficácia restrita das terapias sistêmicas frente aos tumores
resistentes e elevada sobrecarga aos gastos públicos em ambas as faixas etárias, o
desenvolvimento de estratégias terapêuticas mais acessíveis para superar a
quimiorresistência transcende a pesquisa básica, consolidando-se como uma necessidade
de saúde pública.
Nesse cenário de alta demanda clínica, o reposicionamento de fármacos se destaca
como uma estratégia translacional altamente vantajosa. Ao propor a utilização de
medicamentos já aprovados para outras indicações, essa abordagem acelera o
desenvolvimento terapêutico e re duz substancialmente os custos, pois dispensa as
extensas fases iniciais de avaliação de toxicidade e farmacocinética (Pushpakom et al.,
2018). A doxazosina, classicamente prescrita para o tratamento da hipertensão arterial e
da hiperplasia prostática benigna, possui um perfil de segurança consolidado e validado
em pacientes adultos, com efeitos adversos hemodinâmicos bem mapeados e facilmente
manejáveis. A aplicabilidade translacional dos nossos achados no HB é respaldada pelo
histórico de segurança pediátrica da doxazosina. Na prática clínica, o manejo da disfunção
miccional infantil (idade média de 7 anos) com este fármaco apresentou alta
tolerabilidade, com apenas 15% dos pacientes relatando efeitos adversos leves, limitados
majoritariamente a queixas de dor epigástrica (10%) (El-Hefnawy et al., 2012) .
Reforçando essa segurança sistêmica, a administração da doxazosina para o tratamento

93

de cálculos de ureter distal em uma coorte de 2 a 14 anos não registrou qualquer efeito
adverso (Aydogdu et al., 2009). O fato de a doxazosina possuir uma janela terapêutica e
de segurança previamente estabelecida facilita os trâmites éticos e metodológicos para a
sua rápida incorporação em futuros ensaios clínicos oncológicos como um medicamento
adjuvante com alvo no TME.
O TME é composto por células tumorais, CAFs, células imunes residentes e
recrutadas e células endoteliais associadas ao tumor , incorporadas à matriz extracelular
(MEC) remodelada (Cogliati et al., 2023) . As células do TME contribuem para
características fundamentais do câncer, como sinalização proliferativa sustentada, escape
de fatores supressores de crescimento, resist ência à morte celular, indu ção de
angiogênese, invasão , metástase, reprograma ção do metabolismo energético e e scape
imune (Hanahan, 2026; Hanahan & Coussens, 2012; Hanahan & Weinberg, 2011). Nesse
sentido, a ativação das HSCs em CAFs representa um evento crítico na evolu ção do
câncer de fígado. Enquanto em um fígado saudável essas células permanecem em estado
de quiescência, armazenando vitamina A e mantendo a homeostase tecidual, a sinalização
oncogênica persistente e o ambiente inflamatório induzem a sua transdiferenciação em
miofibroblastos/CAFs. Uma vez ativadas, as HSCs passam a secretar proteínas d e MEC
densa (como os colágenos tipo I e III) e citocinas pró-sobrevivência, estabelecendo um
sistema dinâmico que não apenas sustenta o crescimento tumoral, mas também atua como
barreira mecânica e bioquímica à entrada de fármacos convencionais (Affo et al., 2017).
A dinâmica dessa barreira estromal possui particularidades biológicas diretamente
atreladas ao contexto de iniciação de cada tumor. No CHC, a ativação das HSCs em CAFs
decorre majoritariamente do processo inflamatório crônico, resultando em secreção de
citocinas (como TGF -β e IL -6) que retroalimentam vias de proliferação e resistência,
como a PI3K/Akt (Yin et al., 2019) . Por outro lado , no nicho pediátrico do HB, a

94

estruturação desse microambiente está ancorada à sinais remanescentes do
desenvolvimento embrionário e em uma intensa comunicação parácrina , que mantém o
tecido altamente plástico (Q. Zhu et al., 2025). Apesar dessas etiologias contrastantes, as
análises transcricionais integradas nos dois capítulos desta tese revelam que o resultado
clínico final é convergente. No cenário do CHC (Capítulo I), a topologia da rede gênica
evidenciou que o tecido perde a regulação purinérgica homeostática, priorizando o
aumento da expressão de enzimas como ENTPD1 (CD39) e ADA, moldando um
microambiente imunossuprimido. No cenário do HB (Capítulo II), a avaliação do RNA-
seq revelou que os tumores ricos em estroma exibem uma assinatura de transição epitélio-
mesenquimal e dependência da sinalização HGF-MET. A infiltração estromal no HB está
associada à regulação negativa do transportador de influxo SLC31A1 e à superexpressão
das bombas de efluxo ABCC1 e ABCC2, justificando a defesa contra a cisplatina. Ess a
exploração in silico estabelece a base racional para o reposicionamento farmacológico
testado em nossos modelos in vitro.
No contexto da proteção estromal, o reposicionamento de fármacos emerge como
uma estratégia rápida e promissora para desarticular o TME hepático. A doxazosina,
antagonista dos receptores α1 -adrenérgicos, tem demonstrado potencial antifibrótico.
Evidências demonstraram que a doxazosina é capaz de atenuar a fibrose hepática ao
induzir a apoptose em HSCs ativadas e inibir vias de sobrevivência estromal, além de
diminuir a secreção de fatores pró-fibróticos como o TGF-β e o colágeno tipo I (de Sousa,
2021; Muñoz-Ortega et al., 2016; A. -Y. Xiu et al., 2021) . Ao desativar essa maquinaria
de síntese de MEC e aliviar a capilarização sinusoidal, a doxazosina neutraliza a barreira
física e funcional que protege as células tumorais, justificando seu uso para inibir o
estroma reativo tanto no contexto de lesões crônicas do CHC quanto no nicho embrionário
do HB (A. Y. Xiu et al., 2024)

95

Corroborando a literatura recente, os resultados desta tese evidenciam o duplo
efeito terapêutico da doxazosina, que atua de forma simultânea nas células tumorais e nas
HSCs ativadas. No Capítulo I, observou-se que a presença de HSCs nos esferoides mistos
de CHC conferiu maior tolerância ao tratamento com sorafenibe. Contudo, o
cotratamento com doxazosina foi capaz de superar a proteção estromal. Esse resgate da
sensibilidade terapêutica foi mediado pela indução de apoptose via caspase-3 e por
alterações na sinalização purinérgica, com a diminuição da expressão de genes-chave no
metabolismo da adenosina, como NT5E, bem como dos receptores ADORA1 e ADORA2B
(Figura 4). Além disso, a menor expressão dos receptores P1 sugere uma inibição indireta
da cascata PI3K/Akt, uma via de sobrevivência amplamente reconhecida por estar
associada à resistência ao sorafenibe (Aria et al., 2022; Y. J. Zhu et al., 2017).
Figura 4: Desregulação do sistema purinérgico no CHC e efeito da terapia combinada. Análises
transcriptômicas mostram que a superexpressão de NT5E, ADORA1 e ADA associa-se a pior
sobrevida, compondo uma assinatura prognóstica. Em esferoides HepG2 e HepG2/LX -2, o
cotratamento com sorafenibe + doxazosina reduz a expressão de genes adenosinérgicos ( NT5E,
ADORA1, ADORA2A, ADA), supera a proteção estromal (CD73 mantido) e induz apoptose,
evidenciada por ativação de caspase-3 (De Sousa et al., 2026).

96

Com base na perspectiva translacional, os achados do Capítulo II demonstram que
a eficácia da doxazosina na desarticulação do microambiente tumoral estromal não se
limita ao CHC, estendendo -se de forma significativa ao HB. Embora a modulação
específica d o sistema purinérgico não tenha sido avaliada neste estudo, os ensaios
tridimensionais revelaram resultados convergentes em relação à ação da doxazosina. Nos
esferoides mistos de HB, a presença das HSCs protegeu as células tumorais contra a ação
citotóxica do tratamento convencional, a cisplatina. A formação dessa proteção estromal
é impulsionada pela sinalização celular em que as células do HB induzem ativamente a
diferenciação das HSCs residentes em CAFs, dinâmica mediada inclusive pela secreção
de exossomos tumorais (Q. Zhu et al., 2025) . Essa dependência estromal se agrava sob
estresse terapêutico, visto que a própria exposição à quimioterapia intensifica a
comunicação entre as células tumorais e os CAFs, ativando cascatas de sinalização de
sobrevivência que consolidam a quimiorresistência (D. Chen et al., 2025). A introdução
da doxazosina nos esferoides de HB e HB/diHSCs , entretanto, foi capaz de interferir na
resistência e diminuir a viabilidade celular. Reforçando esse potencial, a terapia
combinada de doxazosina e cisplatina resultou em uma redução ainda mais pronunciada
da viabilidade em organoides derivados de pacientes, comprovando sua eficácia em
modelos pré-clínicos de alta complexidade. Esses dados consolidam a premissa de que o
direcionamento terapêutico contra as HSCs ativadas representa uma estratégia promissora
para superar a quimiorresistência hepática.
A avaliação do reposicionamento da doxazosina depende da identificação de seus
alvos diretos no TME . No Capítulo II, a análise por scRNA -seq permitiu mapear sua
distribuição no HB, destacando o ADRA1B como a principal isoforma adrenérgica
expressa no tecido tumoral . Observamos que esse receptor é expresso tanto em uma
subpopulação tumoral de baixa proliferação, enriquecida em marcadores de

97

quimiorresistência e stemness (como ABCC1 e CD44), quanto nas HSCs do estroma .
Esses achados sugerem que a sinalização adrenérgica atua duplamente na progressão
tumoral, induzindo um fenótipo fibrogênico nas HSCs e, garantindo a sobrevivência das
células tumorais tolerantes a fármacos (persister cells ) (He et al., 2024; Oben et al.,
2004). Nesse contexto, a doxazosina exerce um efeito pleiotrópico , além de inibir
mecanismos de resistência na subpopulação tumoral, ela compromete o suporte estromal
ao interferir na sinalização parácrina, como o eixo HGF-MET, e nas interações das células
tumorais com a matriz extracelular (Figura 5).
Figura 5: Dinâmica do TME do hepatoblastoma e sensibilização por doxazosina. O TME
resistente é sustentado pela ativação de HSCs, deposição de MEC e sinalização parácrina (HGF),
promovendo vias de sobrevivência (PI3K/AKT) e efluxo de fármacos (ABCC1). Em modelos 3D,
a doxazosina antagoniza receptores ADRA1B, desorganiza o nicho fibrótico e reduz mecanismos
de resistência estroma-tumor, aumentando a sensibilidade à terapia combinada com cisplatina (De
Sousa et al., 2026).
Apesar do sucesso dessa intervenção em induzir o colapso estromal, a avaliação
do sistema purinérgico evidenciou a plasticidade metabólica e a adaptabilidade do TME.
No Capítulo I, embora o cotratamento com sorafenibe e doxazosina tenha reduzido a
expressão dos genes NT5E, ADORA1 e ADORA2A nos esferoides mistos, essa

98

modulação não se refletiu à nível proteico. Não foram observadas alterações na frequência
de células CD73 +, nem na expressão da proteína na membrana celular . A manutenção
desses níveis proteicos na superfície celular, com o aumento de células CD39+, ilustra
um mecanismo de compensação fenotípica (Antonioli et al., 2013; Moesta et al., 2020) .
Diante do estresse terapêutico, as células do TME prolongam a meia -vida da CD73 já
existente e aumentam a expressão da enzima a montante CD39 em uma tentativa de
restaurar a sinalização de sobrevivência. Além da compensação metabólica, a divergência
entre mRNA e proteína pode ser explicada pelo papel da CD73 como molécula de adesão.
Estudos evidenciam que a CD73 atua como um receptor estrutural, ligando as células
tumorais a componentes da MEC, como fibronectina, laminina e colágeno (Bach et al.,
2023; Wang et al., 2008). Essa função não catalítica conecta os achados dos dois capítulos
desta tese. No Capítulo II, a análise de comunicação celular indicou que as HSCs
contribuem para o suporte estrutural do tumor por meio da secreção de proteínas da MEC.
Nesse contexto, a manutenção da CD73 na membrana dos esferoides mistos (Capítulo I)
sugere que essa proteína esteja associada à rede fibrótica formada pelas HSCs, o que pode
favorecer sua estabilidade na superfície celular e reforçar a barreira mecânica do TME.
Além disso, a modulação transcricional da via adenosinérgica pode não ser suficiente para
desestruturar o estroma reativo. O tratamento combinado com doxazosina induziu
apoptose nas células tumorais e HSCs , sugerindo que sua ação pode contornar os
mecanismos compensatórios do TME.
A investigação dos mecanismos de resistência e compensação foi viabilizada por
uma abordagem translacional, que integrou análises in sílico a modelos tridimensionais
mais complexos. A transição dos ensaios em monocamada (2D) para esferoides mistos
nos permitiu incorporar aspectos importantes do microambiente tumoral, como
organização espacial, barreiras de difusão e interações celulares. Com isso, observamos

99

um aumento na resistência aos quimioterápicos nos esferoides e organoides, evidenciado
pela elevação dos valores de IC50 para o sorafenibe e maior tolerância à cisplatina, indo
de acordo com o que tem sido descrito na literatura (Friedrich et al., 2009). Apesar da
barreira estromal, a doxazosina manteve atividade citotóxica, sugerindo que seu efeito
não é totalmente limitado pela arquitetura do tecido. A avaliação em organoides derivados
de pacientes, que preservam parte da heterogeneidade tumoral, reforça a relevância desses
achados em um contexto mais próximo ao cenário clínico (Broutier et al., 2017) . Esses
resultados indicam que a doxazosina como um tratamento adjuvante representa uma
potencial estratégia antitumoral para o câncer de fígado, cuja aplicabilidade clínica ainda
requer validação em estudos futuros.
O presente estudo possui limitações que devem ser consideradas. Embora os
modelos 3D com HSCs reproduzam a barreira estromal, eles consistem em sistemas in
vitro desprovidos de imunocompetência. A ausência de modelos de cocultivo integrando
células imunes, como linfócitos T, impossibilitou a avaliação de como a desarticulação
estromal induzida pela doxazosina poderia modular a infiltração linfocitária e reverter o
fenótipo imunossupressor do microambiente. Além disso , a ausência de ensaios com
inibidores específicos dos receptores P1 em associação à doxazosina restringe a
confirmação farmacológica direta de que a sinalização adenosinérgica opera como uma
via de escape terapêutico sob estresse. Por fim, em relação ao Capítulo II, embora o estudo
apresente o mapeamento in silic o do microambiente do hepatoblastoma, os achados
derivados da bioinformática ainda carecem de validação experimental direta em nossos
modelos. A comprovação definitiva de alvos delineados pela transcriptômica, em especial
o papel central do receptor ADRA1B, demandará futuras investigações a nível proteico e
funcional, incluindo ensaios de silenciamento gênico, os quais são etapas essenciais para

100
atestar se as predições computacionais se traduzem integralmente no fenótipo celular nas
culturas tridimensionais.
Em conjunto, os resultados deste trabalho reforçam o papel dos CAFs/HSCs na
resistência das neoplasias hepáticas. Em diferentes contextos, observa -se que o tumor
depende de interações com o estroma e de vias de adaptação metabólica, o que pode
contribuir para a limitação das terapias convencionais. Nesse cenário, o reposicionamento
da doxazosina, com ação sobre o compartimento tumoral e o estroma, aponta para uma
abordagem potencialmente relevante, ainda que dependente de validação adicional. A
integração de dados transcriptômicos com modelos 3D contribuiu para a compreensão
dessas interações e oferece suporte inicial para o desenvolvimento de estratégias
terapêuticas mais direcionadas, cujos principais desfechos são apresentados a seguir.

101
6. CONCLUSÃO
Esta tese apresentou os resultados obtidos no estudo do reposicionamento da
doxazosina em modelos 3D de câncer de fígado. Como importantes contribuições para o
tema de pesquisa desenvolvido nesta tese destacam-se:
• O microambiente tumoral hepático atua como um determinante da resistência
terapêutica, impondo barreiras físicas e bioquímicas que sustentam a
sobrevivência celular, independente da etiologia entre o CHC e o HB.
• A desregulação da sinalização purinérgica, caracterizada pela superexpressão de
NT5E (CD73), ADA e receptores P1, constitui uma assinatura prognóstica de
baixa sobrevida global no CHC. A via atua como um mecanismo de resistência
adaptativa e sobrevivência tumoral frente à terapia (Capítulo 1).
• A intervenção farmacológica combinada de sorafenibe e doxazosina desestabiliza
a rede purinérgica tumoral. O cotratamento atenua os mecanismos de
compensação metabólica, promove a regulação negativa de alvos-chave (NT5E e
ADA) e resulta na indução de apoptose (Capítulo 1).
• A barreira fibrótica e a comunicação parácrina estroma -tumor sustentam o
fenótipo quimiorresistente do hepatoblastoma. As abordagens transcriptômicas
evidenciam o receptor ADRA1B como um alvo molecular proeminente e mediador
do crosstalk celular neste microambiente (Capítulo 2).
• A doxazosina atua com um direcionamento duplo, mitigando a evasão intrínseca
da célula tumoral e promovendo a disrupção da barreira fibrótica. Essa
desestabilização estrutural demonstrou -se efetiva na sensibilização dos
organoides de hepatoblastoma à toxicidade da cisplatina (Capítulo 2).

102

7. PERSPECTIVAS
• Avaliar as características morfológicas dos esferoides;
• Analisar se a doxazosina possui efeitos sinérgicos, aditivos ou antagônicos ao
sorafenibe nos tratamentos dos esferoides;
• Determinar a expressão dos genes e proteínas da via de sinalização PI3K/Akt
após o tratamento com doxazosina;
• Avaliar o efeito da inibição de CD73 ou do antagonismo dos receptores P1 na
resposta ao tratamento com sorafenibe e doxazosina nos esferoides de CHC;
• Validar a expressão dos genes de resistência à cisplatina nos esferoides de HB;
• Avaliar a expressão do estroma conforme os subtipos de HB (C1/C2A/C2B);

Protocolo de dissociação de esferoides para citometria de fluxo
Para conseguirmos analisar as células dos esferoides por citometria de fluxo e elas ainda
estarem viáveis após dissociação, desenvolvemos o seguinte protocolo.
Reagentes necessários:
- TrypLE™ Express Enzyme (Gibco, n° cat: 12605028)
- Solução salina tamponada com fosfato (PBS)
- DMEM Low glucose suplementado com 10% SFB, 1% Penicilina/Estreptomicina
- Banho maria a 37°C
- Microtubos de 1,5 mL
- Centrífuga para microtubos, setagem: aceleração 9 e desaceleração 9
- Ponteiras de 200 uL com a ponta cortada
Usamos de 5-6 esferoides por tubo
Após as 48 horas de tratamento dos esferoides, começamos o protocolo
- Aquecer os reagentes no banho maria à 37°C
- Aspirar os esferoides delicadamente com uma ponteira de 200uL cortada na ponta para
não causar atrito nos esferoides;
- Colocar os esferoides em microtubos diferentes de acordo com cada tratamento;
- Adicionar PBS até 1,2 mL no microtubo;
- Centrifugar a 1200 rpm por 10 minutos;

- Descartar o sobrenadante;
- Adicionar 1 mL de PBS nos microtubos;
- Centrifugar a 1200 rpm por 10 minutos;
- Descartar o sobrenadante;
- Adicionar 300 uL de TrypLE™ Express Enzyme por microtubo;
- Colocar os microtubos no banho maria à 37° por 5 minutos;
- Homogeneizar os esferoides rapidamente com a P200 de ponta normal;
- Adicionar 600 uL de DMEM e homogeinizar com a P200;
- Adicionar 500 uL de PBS nos mesmos microtubos;
- Centrifugar os microtubos a 1200 rpm por 10 minutos
Após a dissociação dos esferoides, podemos seguir para os protocolos padrão de

1 | Introduction
Hypercholesterolemia, defined by elevated plasma low- d ensity
lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, is a well- e stablished risk factor not
only for cardiovascular disease (Borén et al. 2022; Steinberg 2013;
Tabas et al. 2015; Boffa and Koschinsky 2019), but also for cognitive
decline and dementia in later life (Kivipelto et al. 2001; Kivipelto
and Solomon  2006; Livingston et  al.  2024; Sparks et  al.  2000,
2003; Zambón et  al. 2010). In fact, in 2024, high levels of blood
LDL cholesterol were officially recognized as a strong midlife risk
factor for dementia (Livingston et al. 2024). This link is supported
by experimental models of hypercholesterolemia, which reveal
that early pathological events such as neuroinflammation and
blood–brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction precede brain impairment
(de Oliveira et al. 2014; de Oliveira, Engel, de Paula, Dos Santos,
et al. 2020; de Oliveira, Engel, de Paula, Melo, et al. 2020; Moreira
et al. 2012; Paul and Borah 2017; Rodrigues et al. 2021, 2024; Streit
and Sparks 1997; Ullrich et al. 2010). A compromised BBB is par-
ticularly critical, as it may permit the entry of peripheral molecules
like LDL into the central nervous system (CNS), a compartment
from which they are normally excluded. Indeed, apolipoprotein B
(ApoB), the primary protein component of LDL, has been detected
in the brain parenchyma of hypercholesterolemic animals, sug -
gesting that LDL influx is a key pathological consequence of BBB
breakdown (Chen et al. 2010; Löffler et al. 2013).
Astrocytes are a highly heterogeneous and widely distributed glial
cell population that plays a critical role in maintaining brain ho-
meostasis and responding to pathological insults in the CNS. As
integral components of the neurovascular unit, astrocytes reg -
ulate BBB integrity, modulate cerebral blood flow, and provide
essential metabolic and trophic support to neurons (Bélanger
et  al. 2011; Bonvento and Bolaños  2021; Herculano- H ouzel and
Dos Santos 2018; Patani et al. 2023; Pellerin and Magistretti 1994;
Zimmer et al. 2017). Owing to their intimate association with cere-
bral vasculature, astrocytes are among the first cells to encounter
circulating factors that traverse a compromised BBB (Patabendige
and Janigro 2023). Consistent with this role, astrogliosis, classically
characterized by increased glial fibrillary acid protein (GFAP) im-
munoreactivity, is a prominent feature of hypercholesterolemic
animal models and frequently co- l ocalizes with regions of BBB
disruption (Ramírez et al. 2011; de Oliveira et al. 2014; de Oliveira,
Engel, de Paula, Dos Santos, et al. 2020).
In this context, in vitro studies have demonstrated that exposure
of cultured astrocytes to lipid- d erived species induces multiple
cellular alterations. For example, treatment with lipolysis prod -
ucts has been shown to increase lipid droplet (LD) accumulation,
upregulate inflammation- r elated gene expression, elevate cellular
stress responses, and enhance cytokine release (Liu et  al. 2015;
Lee et al. 2017). Emerging evidence further suggests that LDs may
act as indirect markers of oxidative stress, as oxidized lipids are
transferred from neurons to astrocytes through neuron–astrocyte
metabolic coupling mechanisms (Liu and Zhang  2014; Smolič
et al. 2021). In parallel, studies examining the effects of native (non-
oxidized) and oxidized LDL (ox- L DL) on brain cells have reported
that LDL exposure in primary cortical neurons and neuronal cell
lines disrupts endolysosomal function, increases amyloid- β pro-
duction, reduces synaptophysin levels, and induces mitochondrial
dysfunction and oxidative stress (Engel et al. 2016; Hui et al. 2012;
Yamchuen et  al. 2017; Farias et  al.  2025). Moreover, incubation
with LDL has been shown to alter astrocyte morphology, although
the specific consequences and mechanisms by which LDL choles-
terol affects astrocytes remain incompletely understood (Dehouck
et al. 1994; Engel et al. 2019; Pitas et al. 1987).
Therefore, BBB dysfunction may permit the entry of LDL cho -
lesterol into the CNS under peripheral inflammatory condi -
tions, such as hypercholesterolemia and metabolic disease. Once
within the CNS, LDL cholesterol can exert neurotoxic effects on
neurons and disrupt glial function. In this study, we investigate
the impact of LDL cholesterol on astrocytes using complemen -
tary in  vitro and in  vivo approaches, focusing on a cell type
that is critical for maintaining brain homeostasis and whose
dysfunction may contribute to the initiation and progression of
neuropathological processes. We hypothesize that astrocytes are
highly sensitive to LDL, and that their response involves a cas -
cade of metabolic and structural changes that contribute to the
pathological brain environment associated with hypercholester -
olemia and contributes to dementia development.

2.2 | Animals and Experimental Design
C57BL/6 wild- typ e and low- den sity lipoprotein receptor (LDLr)
knockout (LDLr −/−) mice were purchased from the Jackson
Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME; RRID:IMSR_JAX:000664,
RRID:IMSR_JAX:002207, respectively), and bred at the Federal
University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS, Porto Alegre, Brazil).
The animals were maintained under a controlled temperature
(23°C ± 1°C) and a 12 h light cycle (lights on at 7:00 a.m.), with
free access to food and water.
In this study, we used male C57BL/6 wild- typ e and LDLr −/−
mice, aged 3 months and 14 months old, divided into four ex -
perimental groups: 3- mon th- old C 57BL/6 wild- typ e mice,
3- month- old LDLr −/− mice, 14- mon th- old C 57BL/6 wild- typ e
mice, and 14- month - old LDLr−/− mice (3–5 animals per group).
The sample size was determined based on previous studies from
our research group in which a two factor animal Genotype ×
Age design was applied (Rodrigues et  al.  2024; de Oliveira,
Engel, de Paula, Melo, et al. 2020 ). Therefore, the study was ini -
tially designed to detect medium- to- lar ge main effects (Cohen's
f = 0.35- 0.40) with α = 0.05 and 1 −β = 0.80, which indicated a
target of approximately six animals per Genotype × Age condi -
tion. Due to practical constraints, the final sample size consisted
of 3–5 animals per group. Post hoc evaluation of the achieved
sensitivity indicated that pairwise comparisons with expected
large effect sizes (Cohen's d = 0.8) corresponded to an average
detectable power of approximately 0.16. Young animals typically
weigh approximately 30–32 g, w hereas middle- age d animals
weigh around 38–43 g. Be tween 3 and 5 animals are housed per
cage (individually ventilated cages; floor area: 501 cm2/77.66 in2;
height: 15 cm; floor dimensions: 30 cm × 16. 7 cm). All animal
procedures were performed following the local ethics commit -
tee and the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of
the National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, MD, USA). Process
numbers: 39781/2020 and 38693/2021. The predefined inclusion
criteria required that all animals be in visibly good health, with
uniform fur, no signs of fighting, and appropriate body weight.
No exclusion criteria were applied beyond these general health
parameters. No animals were excluded, as all met the estab -
lished criteria and remained in good condition throughout the
study. Accordingly, no replacements were necessary. No ran -
domization was performed to allocate animals in the study.
Two experimental cohorts were used: the first ( n = 3–4 animals/
group) was submitted to intracardiac perfusion with 4% PFA,
under previous deep anesthesia with a mixture of ketamine
(80 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/ kg) via intraperitoneally (i.p),
and the brain was collected for immunofluorescence analysis to
evaluate hippocampal astrocytes morphology. A second cohort
of animals was utilized for the evaluation of the gene expression
of astrocytic proteins via quantitative reverse transcription poly -
merase chain reaction (RT- PCR ) (n = 5 animals per group). The an-
imals were euthanized with an overdose of anesthetics (ketamine
150 mg/kg and xylazine 100 mg/kg, administered i.p), followed by
exsanguination. Residual blood components may still be present
in the brain tissue and influence the qPCR analyses. No formal
calculations were conducted to determine the sample size for any
of the animal procedures. The sample size for all animal proce -
dures was determined based on prior studies from our research
group investigating similar variables (de Oliveira et  al.  2014; de
Oliveira, Engel, de Paula, Dos Santos, et al. 2020).

containing 26.2 mM Na HCO3, 40 μ/mL penicillin- str eptomycin,

plating, the cultures were allowed to reach semi- con fluence (24

2.4 | Isolation of LDL Cholest erol From
Human Plasma
Human plasma was collected from donors at Nossa Senhora da
Conceição Hospital. This project was approved by the Ethics
Committee at UFRGS (Ethics Committee Approved Project
Number 43754). The inclusion criteria consisted of healthy adult
individuals without metabolic disorders, following an overnight
fasting period. Exclusion criteria included individuals with pre -
existing medical conditions, pregnant women, and smokers. All
criteria were assessed using a standardized questionnaire ad -
ministered prior to sample collection. As previously reported,
LDL cholesterol was isolated from the plasma using discontin -
uous density gradient ultracentrifugation (de Bem et  al.  2008;

prevent LDL oxidation, and 0.326 g/mL KBr to adjust the den -
sity. Then, 5 mL of the mixture was transferred to a centrifuge
tube, and 5 mL of 0.85% NaCl solution was added to the plasma.
Ultracentrifugation was performed at 191 000 ×g relative centrif-

Cellular metabolic activity was analyzed using a MTT reduc -
tion assay. After 24 and 48 h of LDL cholesterol exposure, cells
were incubated with 0.5 mg/mL MTT (Sigma- A ldrich) dye for
3 h at 37°C, 5% CO 2, and experiments were performed in 96-

Reactive species (oxygen and nitrogen species) were measured

2.19 | Immunofluorescence Staining
and Morphological Analysis
Coronal sections from the mouse hippocampus were stained for
GFAP protein by immunofluorescence. The immunofluorescence
protocol was performed as previously described, with minor mod-
ifications (de Oliveira et al. 2014; de Oliveira, Engel, de Paula, Dos
Santos, et al. 2020). The mice were anesthetized with ketamine-
xylazine (K: 80 mg/kg; X: 10 mg/kg) administered i.p. The ani -
mals were then perfused through the left cardiac ventricle with
0.9% saline solution followed by 4% PFA prepared in 0.1 M PBS,
pH 7.4. Brains were removed and immersed in 4% PFA solution
at 4°C for 24 h, followed by cryopreservation in 30% sucrose solu-
tion in PBS at 4°C. Afterward, brains were frozen in isopentane
at −80°C. Coronal 30 μm sections of the hippocampus were cut
using a Microm HM 525 microtome cryostat (Thermo Scientific-
Germany) at −25°C and stored in 0.1 M PBS with 0.5% sodium
azide at 4°C. The sections were first washed three times with
0.1 M PBS and blocked with 5% horse serum (HS) diluted in 0.1
M PBS containing 2% Triton ×100 (PBS- T x) for 2 h at RT. After
this procedure, the sections were incubated overnight at 4°C
with the primary antibody mouse anti- G FAP (Sigma- A ldrich,
G3893, RRID: P14136, 1:400) in 1% HS diluted in 0.5% PBS- T x.
The sample sections were rinsed (3×) with 0.1 M PBS and incu -
bated with fluorescent secondary antibody, anti- m ouse Alexa
488 (Invitrogen, A11001, RRID: AB_2534069, 1:400) in 1% HS
diluted in 0.5% PBS- T x for 2 h at RT. Finally, the samples were
washed three times with PBS and incubated with DAPI (Thermo
Fisher Scientific, Cat#D1306, RRID: AB_2629482, 1:1000) for 5
min. After three more washes, the sections were mounted with
CC/Mount (Tissue Mounting Medium)- S igma- A ldrich Cat.
n° C9368 and coverslipped. Briefly, the images were captured
using an OlympusFV1000 laser- s canning confocal microscope.
Approximately, 12–15 confocal sections of 1 μm thickness par -
allel to the coverslip (xy sections) were taken with an ×40 ob -
jective (Olympus, U plan- a pochromatic, UPLSAPO40X) and 3×
zoom on the ×40 objective (resolution of 1024 × 1 024 px, field
size of 317.3 × 3 17.3 μm, scanning speed of 4us/px, and pinhole
aperture of 110 μm). Astrocyte morphology was then assessed
using the Simple Neurite Tracer (SNT) plugin for Fiji- I mageJ
(RRID:SCR_002285; http:// rsb. info. nih. gov/ ij/ ). As a selection
criterion, each GFAP analyzed included a single DAPI- s tained nu-
cleus. Parameters such as total process length and total number of
processes were used to assess changes in cell morphology between
experimental groups. To evaluate astrocyte morphology complex-
ity, we have also performed the Sholl Analysis. In this analysis,
skeletonized astrocytes were used as outcomes to create concen-
tric circles around the cell nucleus and measuring the number of
times each astrocyte branch intersects each circle. In this study,
the interval between concentric circles was set at 2 μm for all cells.
The results were then presented in an XY graph, where the aver-
age number of intersections per group was plotted as a function of
the distance from the cell nucleus (Sholl 1953; Ferreira et al. 2010).
Approximately 15- 2 0 astrocytes were analyzed per animal.
2.20 | Statistical Analysis
All data were verified using the Normal (Gaussian) distribution
test, followed by the Shapiro–Wilk normality test to test the dis -
tribution. In the in vitro study, the dataset (n's) that passed the
normality test received a one- w ay analysis of variance (ANOVA)
followed by Dunnett's post hoc multiple comparisons, and n's
that did not pass the normality test received Kruskal–Wallis test
(nonparametric test) followed by Dunn's post hoc multiple com-
parisons. The in  vivo data are expressed as mean ± standard
deviation (SD) and were analyzed by two- w ay ANOVA followed
by using Duncan's post hoc test, without multiple comparison
adjustments. For the in vitro experiments, the reported n (typi -
cally n = 3 ) corresponds to the number of independent biological
experiments, where each replicate was performed on a different
day or using a different cell passage. Each data point shown in
the graphs represents one independent biological sample. Data
are presented according to the graphical representation used.
Dot plots show individual samples with horizontal lines or bars
indicating the mean, and error bars representing the SD when
applicable. Box plots depict the median, interquartile range
(IQR), and minimum–maximum values. For the in vivo exper -
iments, the small sample size ( n = 3 –5) is a limitation inherent
to exploratory studies with genetically modified animal models,
constrained by ethical and financial resources. Results were
considered significant when the p- v alue was less than 0.05, and
were demonstrated by “*.” In addition, we considered a statisti -
cal tendency when p- value ≤ 0.1. The statistical tendencies were
demonstrated by “#”. When normalization was applied, the con-
trol group was used as the reference. In these cases, all values
from the experimental groups were divided by the mean value
of the control group, resulting in the control being expressed as
100%. Sholl analysis data were analyzed using the R statistical
software (version 4.3.2, http:// www. r- proje ct. org/ ). Outliers
were defined, and then, excluded after analysis. All other statis -
tical analyses and graphs were performed in GraphPad Prism 8
for MacOS (version 8.02) statistical software, and Statistic soft -
ware package (Stat- S oft Inc., Tulsa, OK, USA).

performed GFAP immunofluorescence and quantified astro -
cytic morphology parameters using the SNT plugin in ImageJ.
Representative images of astrocyte morphology per group are
shown in Figure  7a. Using Sholl analysis to evaluate astro -
cytes complexity, the two- w ay ANOVA revealed a marginal
effect of genotype on astrocyte morphological complexity
(F(1,11) = 3.935, p = 0 .072), in the hippocampal region CA3
(Figure  7b,c). Analysis of the number of astrocytic processes
demonstrated a significant main effect of age ( F(1,11) = 10.704,

LDLr−/− mice exhibited a significantly greater number of as -

(Figure 7d). In contrast, no significant effects of genotype or age
were observed for astrocyte branch length in the CA3 region
(Figure  7e). Consistent with these findings, no significant dif -
ferences in astrocyte number of processes or branch length were
detected in the Cornu Ammonis 1 (CA1) or dentate gyrus (DG)
hippocampal regions (Figure S2 ).
We next examined the hippocampal gene expression of astro -
cytic markers in young and middle- a ged C57BL/6 wild- t ype and
LDLr−/− mice. Two- w ay ANOVA revealed no significant main

observed in LDLr −/− mice. Finally, aquaporin- 4 ( AQP4) ex-

pression compared with age- m atched C57BL/6 mice at 3 months
of age (** p = 0 .046970), a difference that was no longer evident
at 14 months of age.

have investigated the impact of excess cholesterol on CNS cells
(Engel et al. 2016, 2019; Hui et al. 2012; Ioannou et al. 2019; Pitas
et al. 1987; Shie et al. 2004). In this sense, we believe that the im-
pairment of the BBB that can occur due to hypercholesterolemia
may trigger the extravasation of LDL cholesterol into the brain pa-

investigated the effects of LDL cholesterol on astrocytes.
Considering previous works, we chose the LDL cholesterol con -
centrations and exposure times (Engel et  al.  2016, 2019; Hui
et al. 2012; Smolič et al. 2021; Farias et al. 2025). In addition to cho-
lesterol and cholesteryl esters, LDL particles also carry other lipids,
including triglycerides and phospholipids. Therefore, we aimed to
investigate whether the neutral lipid content of LDL, specifically
triglycerides, can contribute to the formation of intracellular LDs.
Importantly, astrocytes presented intracellular accumulation of
lipid species after being challenged with LDL cholesterol. Several
conditions predispose to the formation of LDs, such as inflam -
matory processes, mitochondrial defects, aging, and extracellular
lipids, which coincidentally are conditions previously described in
AD (Hu et al. 2017). Of particular importance, LDs have already
been observed in neurons of the hippocampus and cortex of pa -
tients with AD (Gómez- R amos and Asunción Morán 2007). Next,
we analyzed the positive LYRS+ by Lysotracker Red staining,
which labels acidified compartments. We performed this labeling
because Marschallinger et  al.  (2020) demonstrated that a novel,
age- a ssociated, LD- r ich microglial cell, “LDAM,” exhibits an accu-
mulation of dysfunctional lysosomal deposits, impaired phagocy-
tosis, and release of pro- i nflammatory mediators. Furthermore, in
cortical neurons incubated with apoB- cho lesterol, endolysosomal
dysfunction was associated with increased deposition of amyloid-
beta (Aβ) and hyperphosphorylated tau (Hui et al. 2012). However,
our findings revealed no significant differences between experi -
mental conditions, suggesting that LDL exposure does not alter the
number of acidified compartments in astrocytes. Further investi-
gations are needed to evaluate additional lysosomal parameters,
including organelle pH, size, subcellular localization, enzymatic
activity, and the expression of hydrolases and classical lysosomal
and endosomal markers. These analyses will help to better eluci-
date the impact of LDL on astrocyte function.
Moreover, as the concentration of LDL- cho lesterol increased,
we observed a significant reduction in the gene expression
of LDLR, HMGCR, and SREBF1. However, the functional
implications of these changes, and whether they represent
adaptive or pathological responses, remain to be fully eluci -
dated. On one hand, the coordinated downregulation of LDLR
and HMGCR is consistent with classical feedback inhibition,
an expected adaptive response to increased intracellular

maladaptive under chronic stress. For example, reduced
LDLR expression may limit cholesterol overload but could
also impair processes beyond lipid handling. Because LDLR
contributes to Aβ clearance in the brain (Basak et al.  2012),
its persistent downregulation could favor Aβ accumulation, a
hallmark of neurodegenerative pathology. In this context, our
observation that APOE mRNA expression also tended to de -
crease is noteworthy, although it contrasts with in vivo studies
in which hypercholesterolemia increased ApoE protein levels
in rabbit cortex (Sparks et al.  1995), underscoring key differ -
ences between simplified in vitro systems and complex in vivo
environments. Recognizing these limitations, future studies
employing pharmacological or genetic manipulation of these
pathways will be essential to establish causality and to dis -
tinguish truly adaptive responses from emerging pathological
consequences.
Given that, our next question was whether astrocytes once ex -
posed to LDL cholesterol exhibit changes in CD36. CD36, a
class B scavenger receptor also known as fatty acid translocase,
has been studied in inflammatory conditions such as athero -
sclerosis, ischemic brain injury, and AD (Kim et al.  2008). The
scavenger receptor family recognizes danger- a ssociated mo -
lecular patterns and expression of CD36 mediates cell- s pecific
responses such as inflammatory responses, phagocytosis of
apoptotic cells, fatty acid transport across the BBB, and lipid
uptake, leading to activation of PPARγ transcriptional path-
ways (Canton et al. 2013; Silverstein and Febbraio  2009; Ioghen
et al. 2021). In astrocytes, the inflammatory mediator CD36 has
been implicated as a novel mediator of injury- i nduced astroglio-
sis and scar formation in stroke, with the hypothesis that CD36
is required for GFAP expression (Bao et al.  2012). In addition,
LCFA and lipoproteins such as LDL and ox- L DL are ligands for
CD36 (Park  2014). In the atherogenic process, the CD36 recep -
tor mediates the recognition and internalization of ox- L DL in
immune system cells (e.g., macrophages) and triggers signal -
ing cascades for pro- i nflammatory responses (Bao et al.  2012;
Park  2014). Exposure to 300 μ g/mL LDL for 48 h p romoted an
increase in CD36 levels. This phenomenon can be explained by
the fact that isolated native LDL cholesterol may contain frac -
tions of ox- L DL, and in the more extended incubation period,
this fraction may be internalized.
Astrocytes are essential CNS cells for glucose uptake (Pellerin
and Magistretti  1994; Pellerin  2018). Therefore, we also mea -
sured parameters related to glucose and energy metabolism.
Our results showed that when cells were incubated with LDL
cholesterol, the glucose analog (2- N BDG) uptake was not signifi-
cantly altered. However, there is a tendency for absorption to de-
crease after 48 h of exposure to 300 μg/mL LDL. This potential
alteration in glucose uptake should be further investigated, as
decreased glucose uptake may be related to the metabolic state
of the cells, because this decrease should also reduce the pro -
duction of lactate, an essential nutrient for neurons. We can
speculate that higher concentrations of LDL cholesterol may
interfere with glucose transport via glucose transporter type 1
(GLUT- 1 )  present in the membrane. After 24 h of exposure to
300 μ g/mL LDL, astrocytes showed a tendency to reduce the
expression levels of the SLC1A3 gene, and after 24 h of incuba -
tion with the 300 μg/mL of LDL, the expression of the SLC1A2
gene tended to increase. In this regard, recently, it was reported
that a mouse model of brain oxysterol imbalance, especially the
elevated levels of 27- h ydroxycholesterol, displays a downregu -
lation of glutamate transporters in the hippocampus (Spanos
et  al. 2024). This deregulation tendency of SLC1A3 and alter -
ations in SLC1A2 expression may indicate an impairment in
glutamate reuptake, which could contribute to synaptic dysreg -
ulation in hypercholesterolemia.
Our findings indicate that LDL cholesterol exposure induces func-
tional alterations in astrocytes that extend beyond disruptions in
cholesterol homeostasis. Changes in glucose uptake tendencies
and glutamate transporter expression suggest that LDL affects
core astrocytic functions critical for neuronal support. These
functional alterations are accompanied by molecular evidence of
astrocytic activation, as reflected by increased GFAP mRNA ex -
pression in LDL- t reated C6 cells. Specifically, exposure to 300 μg/
mL LDL increased GFAP gene expression at 24 h, whereas treat-
ment with 50 μg/mL LDL led to a significant upregulation at 48
h, revealing a concentration- a nd time- d ependent response. This
pattern is consistent with previous reports showing that deleteri-
ous stimuli induce GFAP expression in C6 cells (Shu et al.  2011;
Chao et al. 2015), supporting the interpretation that LDL triggers
a classical astrocytic stress response.
The MTT reduction assay was used to study cell metabolic ac -
tivity. The MTT reagent can cross cell and mitochondrial mem -
branes, and its intracellular reduction is mainly mediated by
oxidoreductase, dehydrogenase, and electron donor enzymes
(Ghasemi et al.  2021). At both exposure times, 300 μg/mL LDL
cholesterol increased reagent reduction, although this effect
reached statistical significance only after 24 h of exposure. The
finding observed with 300 μg/mL LDL suggests that elevated
LDL cholesterol levels may enhance metabolic activity in astro -
cytes. However, it is essential to highlight that the formazan for-
mation reaction has many limitations because other species can
reduce MTT, and it is a low- s pecificity reagent that translocates
to different cellular compartments (Ghasemi et al. 2021 ).
LDL cholesterol appears to elicit a transient oxidative stress
response in astrocytes that is followed by activation of pro -
tective mechanisms. Cells incubated with LDL accumulate
intracellular lipids that may favor β- o xidation, a metabolic
shift potentially linked to pro- i nflammatory states. Compared
with neurons, astrocytes are relatively resistant to oxidative
stress (Bélanger et al.  2011; Wilson  1997). LDL exposure pro -
moted an immediate oxidative challenge, as evidenced by
increased levels of ROS within the first 30 min. In vitro stud-
ies previously published by our group using endothelial cells
(Hort et al.  2014) and macrophages (Straliotto et al.  2013) also
demonstrated increased reactive species generation after 1 h

of exposure to oxidized LDL. As ROS are generated rapidly
and have a very short half- l ife in biological systems, the early
increase in ROS represents a transient kinetic peak rather
than sustained accumulation. In the present study, after 24
h of exposure to LDL cholesterol, ROS production remained
unchanged, whereas a significant decrease in SOD activity
was observed. After 48 h, both SOD activity and ROS levels
remained unchanged. SOD was selected as a representative
antioxidant enzyme indicative of a complex and coordinated
cellular antioxidant response, as cellular antioxidant defense
relies on the integrated action of multiple enzymatic and non -
enzymatic systems. Accordingly, we hypothesize that the re -
duction in SOD activity observed after 24 h of exposure may be
related to an early oxidative stress event. We further propose
that, at this time point, astrocyte cultures do not exhibit de -
tectable increases in reactive species due to the action of other
antioxidant mechanisms independent of SOD activity. After 48
h, the recovery of SOD activity suggests the reestablishment of
its contribution to the cellular antioxidant response. As our
experimental design compares groups within each time point,
we cannot definitively distinguish between a true restoration
of SOD activity in LDL- t reated astrocytes as part of a compen -
satory antioxidant response and/or time- d ependent changes
in baseline SOD activity in the control group. Supporting this
interpretation, we also observed an increase in NRF2 mRNA
expression following LDL exposure, indicating activation of
endogenous cellular stress- r esponse pathways. We propose
that this temporal pattern reflects activation of the nuclear
factor erythroid 2- r elated factor 2- a ntioxidant response ele -
ment (Nrf2- A RE) axis, which promotes the transcription of
antioxidant enzymes and restores redox balance (Sigfridsson
et  al.  2018; He and Hewett  2025). We evaluated NRF2 gene
expression at 24 h as a general marker of pathway engagement
rather than as a precise temporal readout of early activation.
We fully agree that detailed temporal analyses of NRF2 acti -
vation - pa rticularly at very early time points ( ≤ 1 h ) - r equire
dedicated experimental protocols, including assessment of nu -
clear translocation and transcriptional activity, and remain an
important direction for future studies. Increased SOD activity,
in particular, would be effective in dismutating the superoxide
radicals detected in our assays. The apparent discrepancy with
our previous in vivo findings (de Oliveira et al.  2014), where
LDLr−/− mice exhibited impaired glutathione peroxidase
activity and altered glutathione (GSH) levels, actually sup -
ports this interpretation. In the complex in vivo environment,
multiple cell types experience chronic hypercholesterolemia-
induced stress, creating sustained demand for antioxidant
defenses that eventually become overwhelmed. In contrast,
our controlled in vitro system allows astrocytes to mount an
effective compensatory response through their intrinsic an -
tioxidant machinery. This demonstrates that astrocytes pos -
sess robust protective capabilities that can respond to acute
LDL exposure, but these same mechanisms become insuffi -
cient under chronic pathological conditions. These findings
highlight the importance of considering both the temporal
dynamics and the complexity of the cellular environment
when interpreting oxidative stress responses in hypercholes -
terolemia. This interpretation is supported by reports that SH-
SH5Y incubated with 300 μg/mL LDL cholesterol for 1 and 24
h exhibited oxidative stress (Engel et al.  2016). In summary,
astrocytes exhibit some resistance to oxidative stress. After
a short incubation period with LDL cholesterol, there is the
generation of ROS, which does not persist with longer incuba -
tion times, likely due to the action of antioxidant mechanisms.
Our oxidative stress findings reveal a complex temporal pat -
tern that provides important insights into astrocyte adaptive
responses to LDL cholesterol exposure.
Exposure to LDL cholesterol alone does not appear to trigger
proliferation in astrocyte cultures. In some situations, such as
traumatic brain injury, where BBB dysfunction and plasma ex -
travasation into the brain occurs, some astrocytes acquire a pro -
liferative reactive phenotype (Alluri et  al.  2015; Liddelow and
Barres  2017). First, cell density was measured using the SRB
staining method. After 24 h o f LDL exposure, both exposures
appeared to reduce the binding of the dye to basic amino acid
residues; however, the differences were not statistically signifi -
cant. Ki- 6 7 levels were then measured, demonstrating that LDL
cholesterol did not alter the proliferative profile under these
conditions. In our experimental model, exposure to LDL choles -
terol did not alter the proliferation levels of the astrocyte culture,
confirming other studies showing that the reactive astrocytic
phenotype does not always promote proliferation (Liddelow and
Barres 2017).
Our findings demonstrated that, following the longest incuba -
tion period with LDL, the astrocyte lineage did not exhibit signif-
icant changes in apoptosis or late apoptosis/necrosis. Therefore,
LDL- c holesterol at this concentration does not appear to affect
cell death- r elated parameters. A previous study evaluated cell
death parameters in C6 cells after incubation with 27- O HC and
demonstrated that starting at a concentration of 10 μM, 27- O HC
induced early and late apoptosis in C6 cells (An et al.  2017). In
LDLr−/− mice, an increase in neuronal apoptosis was observed
in the CA3 region of the hippocampus, visualized by the co-
localization of caspase 3 (mediator of neuronal death) and NeuN
(neuronal marker). However, caspase 3 and GFAP colocalization
was not verified in these animals (de Oliveira, Engel, de Paula,
Melo, et al. 2020).
Ideally, the concentration of LDL used in vitro should reflect
the physiological levels present in the brains of humans or
mice with hypercholesterolemia, which would substantially
enhance experimental rigor. However, such values remain
unknown, as LDL is not normally found in the CNS and its
concentration under pathological conditions of BBB disrup -
tion has not yet been quantified. For this reason, the LDL
concentration adopted in our study followed methodological
precedent established by previous investigations examining
LDL effects on CNS cells (Hui et al.  2012; Moreira et al.  2012;
Engel et al.  2016, 2019; Farias et al.  2025). These studies pro -
vide the most biologically relevant reference range currently
available for in  vitro exposure. Nonetheless, the absence of
direct measurements of LDL penetration into the hypercho -
lesterolemic brain represents an important limitation. Future
studies employing fluorescently or radioactively labeled LDL
particles in LDLr −/− mice will be crucial to quantify the ex -
tent of LDL entry into the CNS during BBB breakdown. Such
experiments will help establish physiologically relevant LDL
concentrations for in vitro studies and improve translational
accuracy in modeling hypercholesterolemia- i nduced neurobi -
ological changes.

The primary limitation of our in vitro study is the use of the
high- pa ssage C6 glioma cell line, a transformed model that
may not fully recapitulate the complex behavior of primary as -
trocytes. Nevertheless, the selection of this model was deliber -
ate, driven by two key factors: First, its use aligns with the 3Rs
principle (Reduction), enabling a comprehensive mechanistic
analysis with a significant decrease in the number of animals
required for the in  vivo component. Second, higher passage
C6 cells tend to display more astrocyte- l ike characteristics, in -
cluding functional responses that closely parallel those of pri -
mary astrocytes (Galland et al.  2019; Lee et al.  1992), thereby
supporting their validity for studying cellular responses to
LDL cholesterol. To mitigate the risk of phenotypic drift, we
strictly limited the use of the cells to a maximum of five pas -
sages after thawing and confirmed that the line is not listed
in the ICLAC Register of Misidentified Cell Lines. Beyond
the model choice, the acute exposure paradigm used in our
experiments may also contribute to the lack of statistical sig -
nificance observed in some effects. Given that astrocytic re -
sponses to chronic lipid challenges may require longer periods
to fully manifest, future studies will include extended incuba -
tion times to better characterize the long- t erm effects of LDL
on redox balance and metabolic function.
Our in  vivo data demonstrate pronounced astrocytic morpho -
logical alterations in middle- a ged LDLr −/− mice, particularly
within the hippocampal CA3 region. These changes are con -
sistent with astrocytic hypertrophy and suggest a reactive phe -
notype associated with disrupted lipid metabolism (Owasil
et al.  2020; Dai et al.  2023). Previous studies have reported in -
creased astrocyte density in the hippocampus of LDLr −/− mice
(de Oliveira et al. 2014; de Oliveira, Engel, de Paula, Dos Santos,
et al.  2020) and have identified age- d ependent heterogeneity in
astrocytic reactivity profiles (Clarke et al.  2018; Lee et al. 2022).
Previous studies from our research group have demonstrated
elevated GFAP immunoreactivity in young LDLr −/− mice com-
pared with wild- t ype controls (de Oliveira et al. 2014; de Oliveira,
Engel, de Paula, Dos Santos, et al.  2020), indicating early bio -
chemical signatures of astrocyte activation. In the present study,
we extended these observations by moving beyond GFAP immu-
noreactivity to quantify astrocytic morphological complexity,
using Sholl analysis, and parameters of astrocytic morphology.
Importantly, we show that astrocytic morphology is altered by
age and is region specific: While biochemical markers of acti -
vation emerge early, more pronounced structural alterations,
such as increased process number, appear later and are pref -
erentially localized to the CA3 hippocampal region. Together,
these findings support a model in which astrocytic reactivity in
FH represents a progressive event, evolving from early biochem-
ical changes to more complex morphological remodeling with
aging. However, these in  vivo findings should be interpreted
with caution due to the small sample size. Furthermore, while
these morphological changes are significant, their direct func -
tional consequences for neuronal health and cognition remain
to be established and require further investigation.
Also, studies involving LDLr −/− mice have shown that these
animals exhibit impairments in the BBB (de Oliveira, Engel,
de Paula, Dos Santos, et al.  2020 ; de Oliveira, Engel, de Paula,
Melo, et  al.  2020), and microgliosis that worsens with age
(Rodrigues et  al.  2024). In this investigation, two astrocyte
markers, the glial water channel AQP4 and the Ca 2+- binding
protein S100B, demonstrated alterations mainly due to aging.
AQP4 is abundant in the endfeet of astrocytes that are in con -
tact with cerebral vasculature and pia; this isoform of aqua -
porin, an integral transmembrane protein, is involved with
water- c onduction and our levels of expression are associated
with reactive gliosis (Owasil et  al.  2020 ; Dai et  al.  2023).
Studies have indicated that the levels of expression of AQP4
increased in mouse models of AD and in humans with the dis -
ease, a situation that may favor the reported disturbances in
water homeostasis and increased BBB permeability (Wilcock
et al.  2009). We previously observed an increased immunore -
activity of this protein in the hippocampus of LDLr −/− mice
(de Oliveira et  al.  2014). In contrast, herein, we found a de -
creased gene expression of AQP4 in 3- m onth- o ld LDLr −/−
mice. In addition, we also observed that both aged wild- t ype
and LDLr −/− mice present a reduction in the mRNA levels
of AQP4 in the hippocampus. Then, these changes can gen -
erate functional consequences, such as causing an imbalance
in the regulation of water flow and altering the permeability
of the BBB. Expressed mainly in astrocytes, S100B is an es -
sential cytoskeleton component (Barateiro et  al.  2016). We
observed increased S100B mRNA levels in the hippocam -
pus of aged wild- t ype mice. In aging, the S100B expression
showed regional specificity; however, the functional conse -
quences of these specificity alterations remained unknown
(Rodríguez et al. 2014 ).
The selection of 3- a nd 14- m onth- o ld mice was strategically
based on clinical relevance (Zambón et al.  2010) and our previ -
ous characterization of the LDLr−/− model (Moreira et al. 2012;
de Oliveira, Engel, de Paula, Melo, et  al.  2020; Rodrigues
et  al.  2024). Fourteen months represents middle age in mice
(Dutta and Sengupta  2016), corresponding to a period of in -
creased cognitive vulnerability in patients with FH, whereas
3 m onths reflects an early stage of pathology. Notably, our prior
studies have shown that LDLr−/− mice already exhibit BBB dys-
function, neuroinflammation, astrogliosis, oxidative stress, and
memory deficits at this young adult stage (de Oliveira et al. 2014;
de Oliveira, Engel, de Paula, Dos Santos, et al. 2020; de Oliveira,
Engel, de Paula, Melo, et al. 2020). By combining these two time
points, the present study allows assessment of the temporal evo-
lution of astrocytic responses to hypercholesterolemia, distin -
guishing early alterations from age- d ependent changes that may
contribute to cognitive decline in middle- a ged FH.
Although previous studies have examined the effects of LDL
on glial cells (Chen et  al.  2024 ; Niu et  al.  2025), the present
work substantially advances the field by focusing specifically
on astrocyte responses in the context of FH, a mechanism that
remains insufficiently explored. By combining complemen -
tary in  vitro and in  vivo approaches, we provide one of the
first systematic characterizations of astrocyte- s pecific meta -
bolic, oxidative, and functional adaptations to LDL overload.
Our data demonstrate that elevated LDL cholesterol induces
a coordinated astrocytic reprogramming, characterized by
LD accumulation, downregulation of genes involved in cho -
lesterol synthesis and uptake, upregulation of CD36 at higher
concentrations and longer exposures, and the activation of a
transient oxidative stress response marked by early ROS gen -
eration followed by compensatory antioxidant mechanisms.

These metabolic alterations are accompanied by increased
GFAP gene expression and changes in glutamate transporter
expression, suggesting that LDL exposure impacts astrocytic
reactivity and neurotransmitter homeostasis. Extending these
findings in vivo, we show that hypercholesterolemia alters as -
trocytic morphology in an age- a nd region- d ependent manner,
challenging the concept of uniform astrogliosis and highlight -
ing the progressive nature of astrocytic dysfunction in aging
hypercholesterolemic brains. Taken together, our findings
identify astrocytes as key cellular mediators of cholesterol-
induced brain dysfunction and provide new mechanistic in -
sight into how peripheral hypercholesterolemia can disrupt
central nervous system homeostasis, with potential implica -
tions for neurodegenerative disease risk and progression.

ABSTRACT
Bezafibrate (BZF) is a drug that reduces cholesterol and triglyceride levels in the blood. Research indicates that
BZF, through activation of PPAR receptors, regulates the expression of genes involved in lipid homeostasis,
inflammation, cell differentiation, and proliferation. This study investigated the in vitro and in vivo effects of BZF
on activated hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) and on carbon tetrachloride-induced liver fibrosis in mice. After 72 h of
treatment in vitro, BZF decreased cell proliferation, reversed the phenotype, decreased cell contraction, and
induced autophagy. In addition, BZF promoted a protective effect on tetrachloride-induced liver fibrosis in mice,
through antifibrotic actions. These findings suggest that BZF may have a potential antifibrotic effect, which could
emerge as a possible new therapy for the treatment of liver fibrosis.
1. Introduction
Hepatic fibrosis (HF) is associated with lesions resulting from viral
infections, alcohol abuse, steatosis, metal intoxication, and hereditary
diseases leading to the accumulation of collagen-rich fibrotic matrix
and, in more advanced stages, liver failure and death (da Silva et al.,
2020; T¨or¨ok, 2008). Therefore, it is considered a public health emer -
gency, considering the increased incidence of HF, which currently rep -
resents one of the ten most common causes of death in the world
(Balasundram et al., 2006; de Souza Basso et al., 2021).
HF is caused by the proliferation and activation of hepatic stellate
cells (HSCs), and an inability to store vitamin A in cytoplasmic lipid
droplets, as well as an increased expression of α-smooth muscle actin
(α-SMA) (Basso et al., 2019; Soon and Yee, 2008). Thus, it is a chronic,
partially reversible disease that, in advanced stages, may cause portal
hypertension, ischemia, and loss of liver function. It is initially triggered
by metabolic changes and inflammatory processes that activate hepatic
fibrosis in response to continuous aggression (Codogno and Lotersztajn,
2014; Hernandez-Gea and Friedman, 2011; Pinzani and Gentilini,
1999).
HSCs reside in the perisinusoidal region together with hepatocytes
and endothelial cells representing 8% of the hepatic cell population.
HSCs present a quiescent phenotype, characterized by the transcription
of adipogenic genes forming lipid vacuoles with retinyl esters and tri -
acylglycerides in their intracellular portion. When submitted to injury,
HSCs start a process of transdifferentiation from the quiescent pheno -
type to the activated state that has myofibroblasts-like properties
(Gabbiani, 2003). The HSCs lose lipid vesicles, increase the proliferation
and initiate the synthesis of collagen and extracellular matrix proteins,
release of inflammatory and pro-fibrotic cytokines. These conditions are
associated with the progression of HF (Guimar ˜aes et al., 2007; Mallat
et al., 2014).

Studies have evaluated the effectiveness of treatment for initial-
phase liver fibrosis in order to prevent lesion progression, reduce
inflammation, and stellate cell activation by controlling the proliferative
response and cell fibrogenesis (Rockey et al., 2019; Trautwein et al.,
2015). Thus, drug repositioning is an alternative for the treatment of HF.
The adverse effects of drugs already approved are known, as clinical
tests were already performed, representing less risk to the health of
patients. Bezafibrate (BZF) is a drug that reduces cholesterol and tri -
glyceride levels in the blood. It belongs to the group of fibrates, which is
a class of amphipathic carboxylic acids, presenting agonist activity for
the peroxisome-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-α) (Mizuno et al., 2017;
Ohmoto et al., 2006).
Research has indicated that treatments aimed at decreasing the
fibroproliferative process, reversing the quiescent phenotype and ECM
accumulation may be more promising for HF. For that reason, PPAR-s
agonist drugs provide a potential therapy for fibrotic diseases as they
induce the differentiation of myofibroblasts and type I collagen protein
(Liu et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2022). Some studies have shown that
bezafibrate may have an effect on liver fibrosis, but they were performed
on cells or animals separately (Ibrahim et al., 2021; Nagasawa et al.,
2006; Nakano et al., 2008). Therefore, the present study sought to verify
the potential antifibrotic effect of BZF in experimental models in vivo
(mouse), in vitro, (cell line of mouse activated stellate cells (GRX) and
human cells (LX-2), where for first time, we can see that bezafibrate can
be used people as an antifibrotic agent in the liver.
2. Materials and METHODS
2.1. In vitro experiments
2.1.1. Cell culture
HSC murine cells (GRX cells line) were obtained from Rio de Janeiro
Cell Bank (BCRJ, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; code: 0180) and the Human LX-
2 cell line was kindly provided by Professor Dr. F´atima Theresinha Guma
(Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul. Cells were maintained in
Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM; Gibco™, USA – 1 g/%)
supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco™, USA), 1%
streptomycin (100 μg/mL) and penicillin (100 U/mL) (Gibco™, USA),
and incubated in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2 at 37 ◦C.
2.1.2. Cell number determination
GRX cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 5 × 103
cells/well and treated with BZF (10, 20, 30, and 40 μϺ) diluted in 0.5%
DMSO (Sinth, 01D1011). GRX cells were also assessed by direct count-
ing using the Trypan blue (Gibco™, USA) exclusion assay. All the ex -
periments used NAC (N-acetylcysteine) 2.5 mϺ as a positive control.
NAC is known as a potent antioxidant because it produces glutathione.
Here we use it as an anti-proliferative agent because is able to decrease
the proliferation of hepatic stellate cells through cell cycle arrest ( Kim
et al., 2001). Outcome assessments were performed after 72 h, always in
triplicate. These concentrations were used because the ingestion of 300
mg of bezafibrate in healthy volunteers have a 2-h peak of 26.7 μM in
plasma (10 mg/L) (Monk and Todd, 1987).
2.1.3. Cytotoxicity assay
In order to evaluate the cytotoxicity of BZF in the cells, a marker of
membrane damage, the lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) enzyme, was
determined in the supernatant of cell cultures. The cells were seeded at a
density of 1 × 104 cells per well in 24-well plates and treated with
different concentrations (30 and 40 μϺ) after 72 h. The experiments
were performed in triplicate. The enzyme activity was measured by the
commercial kit Lactate dehydrogenase (Labtest), according to the in -
structions of the manufacturer. Results are expressed in percentages and
calculated by measuring the absorbance at 492 nm using a microplate
reader.
2.1.4. Detection of lipid droplets
The lipid droplets were analyzed through the oil red technique. The
cells were seeded in 24-well plates at a density of 3 × 103 cells per well,
with 30 μϺ and 40 μϺ concentrations of BZF, after 72 h. The cells were
fixed with 10% formaldehyde and stained with Oil Red O (Sigma, 1320-
06-5). Intracellular lipid accumulation was verified after 30 min, using
an inverted optical microscope. The results were calculated as the ratio
of absorbance and the number of cells. The optical density was 492 nm,
and experiments were performed in triplicates.
2.1.5. Assessment of cell contraction by collagen gel assay
Cell contraction is a typical feature of the transition from fibroblasts
to myofibroblasts. GRX cells were seeded into 24-well plates at a density
of 1 × 105 cells per well, in 4x concentrated DMEM (4 g/%) in a 4 mg/
mL collagen solution. The collagen gels were polymerized for 30 min at
37 ◦C, with treatments or with 2.5 mM NAC. After 24 h, images of each
gel were obtained, and the percentage of the total surface area occupied
in each well was determined. The gel concentration test considers the
diameter occupied by the gel disk in relation to the total size of the well
(set as the 100% value). Therefore, the result shows the area occupied by
the gel in relation to the total area of the well.
2.2. In vivo experiments
2.2.1. Animals
Male BALB/c mice with 8 weeks were kept under specific conditions
of 12 h light-dark cycle, temperature of 22 ± 2 ◦C, and 50–70% hu -
midity. Animals received free access to food and water, were housed in
individually ventilated cages, and acquired from the Center of Biological
and Experimental Models of the Pontifícia Universidade Cat´olica do Rio
Grande do Sul (CeMBE; PUCRS; Brazil). The experimental protocol was
approved by the Animal Use Ethics Committee (CEUA).
2.2.2. Experimental design
In order to evaluate the antifibrotic effect of BZF, the animals at 8
weeks of age were submitted to an experimental protocol of HF induc -
tion. Experimental induction was performed through the periodic
administration of CCl 4 (Liedtke et al., 2013) diluted in olive oil at a
concentration of 1 mL/kg per body weight, injected via I.P. three times a
week for ten weeks. The BZF-treated groups (50 mg/kg and 100 mg/kg)
received the selected doses via gavage twice a week, after 24 h of the
administration of the first dose of the induction protocol. After 72 h of
the last dose, the animals were euthanized, and liver sections and serum
were collected.
2.2.3. Biochemical serum analysis
Blood samples were collected by cardiac puncture and centrifuged
for 10 min at 2000 g at 4 ◦C. Serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was analyzed with a commercial
assay kit, according to the manufacturer’s recommendations (Labtest,
Brazil).
2.2.4. Histopathology liver analysis
The liver samples were fixed in 10% buffered formalin, embedded in
paraffin blocks, cut into 5 μm sections, and stained with hematoxylin
and eosin stain. Liver sections were assessed semiquantitatively ac -
cording to the Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease Activity Score (NAS):
The inflammation score ranges from 0 to 4, 0 = no foci, 1 =<2 foci/200
× , 2 = 2–4 foci/200 × , 3 =>4 foci/200 × . Ballooning ranges from 0 to
2, 0 = none, 1 = few balloon cells and 2 = Many balloon cells/prominent
ballooning. Images were captured using the BMX 43 microscope
equipped with the digital DP73 camera (Olympus Tokyo Japan). In
order to analyze fibrosis, liver sections were stained with Picrosirius Red
(Polysciences, Inc., USA). Liver fibrosis also was semiquantitatively
determined: fibrosis (0–4). Images were captured using the same mi -
croscope previously described.

For immunohistochemistry, the tissue samples were cut into sections
of paraffin-embedded blocks and mounted onto slides. The slides were
dehydrated and the antigen retrieval was performed in citrate buffer ph
= 6.0, and samples were washed in PBS. During the blocking step, the
samples were incubated with 0.1% of Triton and 5% serum in PBS so -
lution for 1 h at room temperature. Primary antibodies, α-SMA and
GAPDH, were incubated at a concentration of 1:200 diluted in a
blocking solution at 4 ◦C overnight. In the next step, the samples were
washed with PBS and incubated for 1 h, with a secondary anti-rabbit
antibody diluted 1:200 in PBS with TritonX 0.1%. After incubation,
the samples were washed with PBS. DAB was used as chromogen and
counterstained with hematoxylin, followed by a rehydration step. The
samples were mounted with DPX and left to dry completely at room
temperature. Images were obtained in the BMX 43 microscope, equip -
ped with the digital DP73 camera. Analyses of the stained areas were
performed by calculating the percentage of the DAB stained area using
the ImageJ software.
2.3. Real-time quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR)
The gene expression of the markers was carried out in both in vitro
and in vivo experiments. In vitro, GRX cells were seeded into 6-well plates
at a density of 2.5 × 105 cells/well and treated with BZF (30 and 40 μϺ)
or NAC 2.5 mϺ. After 72 h, the total RNA was extracted using TRIzol™
reagent (Invitrogen, USA), according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
In the in vivo experiments, the mice liver tissue samples were also
extracted using TRIzol reagent. The mRNA was reversely transcribed
into cDNA, using the GoScript™ Reverse Transcription System kit
(Invitrogen, USA), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The
quantity of cDNA was examined using the NanoDrop 2000 (Thermo
Fisher Scientific). The expression levels were quantified by qRT-PCR,
performed using the StepOne™ Real-Time PCR System (Applied Bio -
systems™, USA). The reaction was catalyzed by the SYBR Green I
(Applied Biosystems™, USA) kit, according to the manufacturer’s in -
structions. The experiments were performed in duplicate and the reac -
tion products were verified by melting curve analysis. Data were
analyzed with glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) as
a normalized gene. Table 1 shows the primer sets used.
2.4. Western blot
Cells lysed using a specific buffer at 12,000 g for 30 min at 4 ◦C. Total
protein concentration was determined by a NanoDrop Lite spectropho -
tometer (Thermo Scientific, USA). Equal amounts of protein (30 μg)
were separated on electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE). The primary antibodies
used were anti-α-SMA and anti-GAPDH (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA)
and the secondary antibody was anti-IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific,
USA). The proteins bands quantification was performed using ImageJ
software.
2.5. Statistical analysis
Results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Data
were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by
the Tukey multiple comparison test. Differences were considered
significant when a p < 0.05 was identified. Statistical GraphPad Prism
Version 5.00 was used as a computational tool to analyze data.
3. Results
3.1. BZF decreases GRX cell proliferation
Firstly, GRX cells were exposed to different concentrations of BZF
(10, 20, 30, and 40 μϺ), NAC 2.5 mM (positive control) and DMSO
(vehicle control) to assess their antiproliferative effects. After 72 h of
treatment, there was a significant difference when the control group was
compared to NAC and all doses of BZF. These results indicate that higher
doses reduced cell proliferation more effectively. Therefore, the 30 μϺ
and 40 μϺ doses were chosen to continue with the experiments (Fig. 1).
3.2. BZF does not induce cell membrane damage
The experiments have shown that there was no significant difference
between the BZF treatment and the control group (Fig. 2). These results
indicate that the decrease in cell number is not related to membrane
damage.
3.3. BZF induces phenotypic GRX cell reversion and increases PPARs gene
expression
The cellular phenotype was evaluated through the presence of lipid
droplets in the cytoplasm. An increase in the presence of accumulation
of lipid droplets was observed in GRX cells treated with BZF (Fig. 3 A).
Results also showed that NAC treatment caused a significant increase in
lipid droplets. These results were confirmed by quantifying the accu -
mulation of lipids by reading the absorbance at 492 nm ( Fig. 3B). The
expression of PPARs family genes, an intracellular lipogenic factor, was
also evaluated. According to our results, there was a significant increase
in the expression of PPAR-γ mRNA (Fig. 3C) in cells treated with BZF in
comparison to the control and DMSO groups, as well as in PPAR-α in the
treatment with 40 μM (Fig. 3D) of BZF. Our control (NAC) increased the
expression of the PPAR- α gene only. NAC, a PPAR- α-only inducer, has
been shown to induce only PPAR alpha and not PPAR-γ mRNA,
corroborating our data. These results indicated a phenotypic reversal of
activated stellate cells.
3.4. BZF decreases the fibrotic status
The main features of activated stellate cells are increased contraction
as well as the production of α-SMA and collagen. Our data showed that
BZF and NAC treatments significantly decrease cell contraction
